title: UDLF Detection Schema v0.2.1
description: Universal Detection Lifecycle Format (UDLF) detection schema. A detection is one threat-idea that may carry multiple logic variants (each in its own language) and be deployed to multiple named targets, each with its own lifecycle stage and runtime mode. Deployment mechanics and secrets are never stored here — UDLF is the deploy-neutral source of truth.

id.description: Unique identifier for the detection (UUID v4).

lifecycle.description: Overall maturity stage of the detection. Also the pre-deployment default inherited by any deployment that omits its own 'lifecycle'.

created_at.description: ISO 8601 date the detection was created (YYYY-MM-DD).

detection_content.description: Detection logic variants. Each entry is one language + its logic. A deployer selects the variant appropriate to a target (e.g. Splunk -> spl). Several entries may share a language (e.g. a tstats-accelerated SPL alongside a raw-log SPL, or one tuned per client); give those an optional 'description' so a human can tell them apart. For language 'sigma', 'logic' is an embedded native Sigma rule object validated against the pinned SigmaHQ schema; for every other language 'logic' is the raw query string.

language.description: Query language of this logic variant. 'sigma' embeds a native Sigma rule object.

description.description: Short human-readable label for this variant, e.g. 'Raw log SPL version' or 'Tuned for client X'. Documentation only — it does not select a variant at deploy time.

logic.description: The detection logic. A raw query string for spl/kql/yara/yara-l/python/sql; an embedded native Sigma rule object when language is 'sigma'.

description.description: Detailed description of what the detection identifies.

implementation_guidance.description: How to implement the detection (data sources to collect, prerequisites, tuning). Free text (multiline). Renamed from v0.2.0 'how_to_implement'.

investigation_guidance.description: Guidance for investigating alerts from this detection. Free text (multiline). Indicative pointers for an analyst or agent, not a rigid step-by-step runbook.

attack_procedures.description: The TTP procedure(s) that trigger this detection — the actual attacker command line(s) or example execution that would cause it to fire. Free text (multiline) for now; may gain structure in a later version.

threat.description: Threat intelligence tagging (MITRE ATT&CK and related).

attack_version.description: ATT&CK release this detection was authored against (e.g. "19"). Documents authoring context; does not gate validation.

technique.description: MITRE ATT&CK technique or sub-technique ID (e.g. T1059, T1059.001).

tactics.description: Tactics linked to this technique. Additive union enum — forward-tolerant across ATT&CK releases.

custom_tags.description: Free-form organizational tags. Keys and values are unconstrained.

tests.description: Validation tests. Each entry names a test framework and carries fields appropriate to it. 'framework' is intentionally open/extensible; the three known frameworks (replay, synthetic, atomic-red-team) are validated conditionally.

framework.description: Test framework. Known values: replay, synthetic, atomic-red-team. Extensible — other values are accepted without framework-specific validation.

expected.description: Optional expected outcome. 'hit' = the detection should fire; 'miss' = benign data must not fire (false-positive test).

data.description: URL to the recorded log data.

technique.description: ATT&CK technique the atomic test exercises.

links.description: Typed relationships to other detections, strategies, or sources. 'type' and 'target' are required; the type-specific fields below are optional and scoped by convention to the type named in their description. The object is closed — 'type' is a closed enum, so a new link kind needs a schema bump anyway, and rejecting undeclared keys catches a misspelt 'license' rather than silently dropping a redistribution obligation.

target.description: The related resource, as a UUID or URI. For a 'derived_from' link to a public source this is a permalink to the upstream rule on its default branch — stable across syncs, unlike a commit permalink. Imports from a customer's own SIEM have no public URL and keep an internal scheme (e.g. 'splunk:<id>').

source_id.description: derived_from: the source's own identifier (e.g. the upstream Sigma or ESCU rule UUID).

source_format.description: derived_from: the format the detection was translated from (e.g. sigma, escu, splunk). Open/extensible.

source_version.description: derived_from: the source's own version — an ESCU/Elastic integer, a Sigma 'modified' date, or a commit SHA. Not the import date.

license.description: derived_from: URL of the licence the source is distributed under (e.g. https://github.com/SigmaHQ/Detection-Rule-License, https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0). A URL rather than an SPDX identifier because it doubles as the attribution link some source licences require on redistribution. Optional in the schema — an import from a customer's own SIEM has no upstream licence — but a translator of public content should always emit it, alongside 'target' and 'modification'.

modification.description: derived_from: prominent notice stating how the source was changed, as required by licences such as Apache-2.0 section 4(b). E.g. 'Translated from Sigma YAML into UDLF v0.2.0; detection logic unchanged.'

deployments.description: Where and how this detection runs. Each entry binds the detection to a 'platform' (the discriminator that selects the logic variant and scopes the free-form 'config' block) and, optionally, a named endpoint. First-class fields are the cross-vendor runtime axes only: platform, mode, optional name/lifecycle. Everything platform-specific (schedule, suppression, rba, vendor round-trip fields) lives in 'config'. Deployment mechanics and secrets (base_url, token, app, owner) live in platform/CI config, never here — they are resolved from the named endpoint.

name.description: Optional friendly name for a specific endpoint (e.g. splunk-prod, splunk-staging). Resolved by the deployer/CI to real infrastructure and secrets. Omit when there is a single endpoint for the platform. Listed first so entries read name-then-platform when one platform has multiple named endpoints.

platform.description: Deployment target — the discriminator. Known values: splunk, splunk-es, splunk-contentctl-v5-6, sentinel, defender-for-endpoint, crowdstrike, sentinel-one, elastic. Selects the logic variant (e.g. splunk-es -> spl, sentinel -> kql) and scopes the meaning of the free-form 'config' block. Usually names a product, but may name a delivery toolchain where that changes the shape of 'config': splunk and splunk-es are built and uploaded as an app by the deployer, while splunk-contentctl-v5-6 hands a contentctl-shaped detection to the contentctl build pipeline instead. A toolchain platform carries the tool version when its format is not stable across major versions — splunk-contentctl-v5-6 targets contentctl v5.6, and a later line would be a sibling value (splunk-contentctl-v6-3), not a redefinition of this one. Note that EDR targets are not scheduled-search platforms — sentinel-one evaluates continuously and its config carries active-response actions rather than a schedule. Intentionally open/extensible: unknown values validate against the common fields only.

mode.description: Runtime behavior of this deployment. alert = runs and generates alerts/notables. warranty = runs against known-good/known-bad data to validate coverage; produces a test result, not an alert. monitoring = runs on a schedule and surfaces non-alerting output for human review (dashboards, risk/RBA contribution, hunt-triage queues, situational awareness); does not alert. disabled = present but not executing. Note: an ad-hoc/manual hunt is not a mode — it is a detection with no 'deployments' entry, executed on demand.

lifecycle.description: Lifecycle stage of this specific deployment. Inherits the top-level 'lifecycle' when omitted.

config.description: Free-form, platform-scoped deployment configuration. Its meaning is set by the sibling 'platform'; this schema validates nothing inside it (additionalProperties: true) so vendor changes never force a UDLF bump. Holds deployment policy and vendor round-trip fidelity that UDLF does not model first-class: e.g. for splunk-es, 'rba' (message/risk_objects/threat_objects), 'schedule' (cron/lookback), 'suppression' (fields/window), 'notable', and 'drilldown_searches'. On import, populate from the vendor export; when authoring new, omit and let the deployer generate what the platform requires. Optional, opt-in sub-schemas describing the known shapes ship separately under schemas/udlf/config/<platform>/v<version>.json. They are deliberately NOT referenced from here — validate against one as a second, explicit pass when you want the block checked. A config block may name the sub-schema revision it was authored against via a 'schema' key (e.g. 'splunk-es::0.1.0'); those revisions carry their own semver line so config shapes version independently of UDLF core.

changelog.description: Append-only, chronological record of notable changes. Placed last as it grows unbounded. Replaces a separate 'updated_at' — the most recent entry's date is the effective last-updated date, and each entry's 'version' ties a change to the release it shipped in. Reference the affected language variant or deployment platform/endpoint in the summary prose.

version.description: Semantic version this change shipped in (e.g. 1.0.0).

summary.description: What changed and why. Reference the affected language variant or deployment target here.
